COMMENTARY To Section 1 The Process Flow Diagram will show the steady state mass balance at the design capacity of the plant. Flows, pressures and temperatures for all significant streams, including utilities, must also be shown.  Pump kick-back lines, drain lines, etc. are not show on the PFD. Normally the only physical properties that needs to be shown on the PFD is density.  Other physical properties are show on the relevant PDS , PDL, Line List, etc. There may be a number of cases, e.g. strong acid plants, where additional Process Flow Diagrams are required to fully define the plant capacity and/or operation. The term “steady state” is understood to apply for “instantaneous design conditions” such as maximum operation, minimum turndown, autothermal condition etc.  These are not true steady state conditions, but represent conditions under which it is necessary to establish mass and energy balances. To Section 3.3 and 3.4 PFD Sketch: Process prepares a PFD sketch from a source , which can be from one or more of the following: • Standard template • Proposal Flow Diagram, which is an Attachment to the Contract • Previous PFD used in another project • Hand sketch Clarity of the presentation is important.  All main process and utility lines must be shown. Grouping and crowding equipment at the expense of clarity should be avoided. Drawings : • The equipment shall be drawn approximately in proportion to the actual sizes, in a sequence of flow from left to right. • Each equipment item including those with duplicate sets is to be shown. • Connectivity lines will be: • Solid thick line for major process lines • Solid thin line for minor process lines and utility lines • Dashed lines for existing equipment • The first page of the set of drawings will show the Project Design Capacity. Drawing Borders and Size : • Standard border showing the vertical block • Non-standard borders may be requested by the Client • Standard size drawing may be metric “A1” or Imperial “D” size Numbering : • PFD drawing number : Refer to 0-PRC-0002: Document Numbering To Section 3.5 Process will calculate the stream data using: • “In house “ software programs, FORTRAN or EXCEL based • Process simulation software, e.g. ASPEN

Commentary To Section 1: The P&ID’s are dynamic documents that progress in detail throughout the duration of a project. During the design phase of a project, the P&ID’s (Piping and Instrumentation Diagram) are used to convey information, primarily from the process engineer to the other disciplines, to assist in the creation of subsequent documents, used for construction or purchasing, that specify the detailed design of the plant.  Examples of these sorts of documents include; equipment data sheets, instrument specification sheets, line lists, pipe isometrics, logic drawings, equipment outline drawings, etc. Later in the project, information is transposed from other project documents, such as the line list and equipment outline drawings to the P&ID’s to provide a summary record of the basic design and specification of the Plant. Pipe isometrics are generally the governing documents for pipe construction and routing, however, for field run pipe, the P&ID’s may be the governing documents, along with pipe routing criteria, if applicable. Operation personnel use the P&ID’s as a concise reference for the relationship of process steps and unit operations, general control scheme overview, instrument number and general location, sample point locations, etc. The P&ID’s are used as the primary document in HazOp studies. To Section 2: Templates Each P&ID drawing should be based on the appropriate technology standard P&ID.  In general, a single drawing of the P&ID is to be limited to one or two unit operations or processing steps as defined by Technology.  Standard P&ID’s have been put together for each Technology such that most unit operations, equipment or processing steps can be added or removed from a project without impacting other P&ID’s, therefore, the layout of equipment within project P&ID’s remains the responsibility of Technology.  This will ensure that development done during a project is portable to other projects or standards with little impact to the overall standardization scheme for Technology P&ID’s. Format Legends: • The first page of the set of drawings will be the Legend.
Drawing Borders and Size: • Standard Aker Kvaerner Chemetics border • Non-standard borders may be requested by the Client • Standard size drawing may be metric “A1” or Imperial “D” size

Section 3.2:  Stage 2 P&ID Information for Line List: The number of steps exchanging information between the line list and PID has been reduced. Basically, all of the information required from the PID’s for the line list is transposed in one step, using Stage 2PID’s.  The line list procedure has been modified to mesh into this concept. Line identifier: The line identifier is the six digit number of the line number, made up of a 4 digit equipment number reference and a 2 digit “serial” number.  The design group will typically work directly on the drawing to assign the logical serial number to lines within a given equipment reference, following P&ID standards.  The line list may be referred to as a check to see what serial numbers have been used and to ensure that numbers have not been duplicated.  Once all lines have been developed on the P&ID, the information will be transposed from the drawing into the list.  The designer may chose to do this on an “as go” basis as systems are completed. Approval: The project engineer approval ensures that the P&ID is complete with respect to the minimum required elements as listed, not for technical “accuracy” in areas outside of his speciality. Section 3.3:  Stage 3 P&ID Information from Stage 3 Line List: The number of steps exchanging information between the line list and PID has been reduced. Basically, all of the information required from the line list is transposed in one step, during the Stage 3 PID development.  The line list procedure has been modified to mesh into this concept. Equipment nozzle tag: • For type C, D, and E equipment, Process will add equipment nozzle tags to P&ID according to typical OTL standards and PDS nozzle schedules showing the letter designator and preliminary nozzle size.  Generally, this will be done before the OTL’s are completed for the project.  Nozzle requirements are generated on the P&ID and on the OTL as a multidiscipline effort.  A standard scheme for tag allocation is the responsibility of the Design group. • For package equipment, Design will assign nozzle tags to the P&ID to match Aker Kvaerner Chemetics standard scheme but the nozzle size will be transposed from Vendor documentation, by the design group.  Vendor drawings will be marked-up to match nozzle tags to Aker Kvaerner Chemetics documentation and standards, by the Design group. Hand valve process requirements: Process will define valve special functionality requirements.  If the details of the valve requirement are fully understood, Process will indicate this by assigning the appropriate valve identification number by selecting the most suitable valve from the Pipe Service List 5-LST- 000X.  If the type of valve required is fully understood, Process will indicate this by assigning the size (optional) and first number of the valve numeric indicator.  For example, if a butterfly valve is best suited, Process will assign X”V2xxx.  If a special function is required but there is no clear most suitable choice on the Pipe Service List, Process will add a note on the engineering layer identifying the service, such as "throttling" or “tight shut off”.  Additional requirements( if any),  such as, "red tag open",  “vent required”, etc. will also be added as notes to the PID.

Section 3.7:  P&ID As Built During the course of construction and commissioning, changes will be initiated on site. The instrument air distribution piping will be such that the air take-off points are located on the top of headers and manifolds, Drain valves will be located at the lowest points. Each instrument air user will be connected via a dedicated isolating ball valve and a dedicated in-line filter/water trap. Impulse tubing will be 1/2" hard drawn seamless 316 stainless steel. Stainless steel fittings will be of imperial sizes. Metric sizes are not acceptable. Stainless steel valves and compression fittings will be used unless the process fluid or the process ambient conditions dictate otherwise. All process connections will be provided with an isolation cock. The maximum length of any impulse tubing will be 15 metres. All impulse lines will be installed with a minimum gradient of one in twelve to ensure that the entire line is self-draining. All stainless steel compression fittings will be selected from the manufacturer and range approved by the Company for the project. Nylon tubing will not be used. Local air distribution manifolds, with a minimum of 25% spare outlet capacity and a drain point with valve, will be used. Instrument Installation Requirements The installation will be arranged to facilitate ease of operation, inspection and maintenance and will incorporate all safety measures necessary to protect operating and maintenance personnel. Installation drawings will be provided for all instrument types. All instruments connected via process impulse tubing will be provided with both primary and secondary isolation. Instrument Mounting All instrumentation will be installed in such a manner that it is serviceable or replaceable without the aid of a ladder or scaffolding. Local indicator instrumentation such as dial thermometers, pressure gauges will be plainly visible and accessible from grade or platform. All instruments connected via process impulse tubing will be provided with an isolation device as close as possible to the process and also with an isolation device as close as possible to the instrument. Instrument mounting brackets will be 316 SS or epoxy coated mild steel. Two-inch (2") pipe brackets will be included in the supply of all instruments with exception of line/flange mounted instruments. All associated mounting bolts and fasteners will be stainless steel.

Commentary To Section 3.6 (Process Logic Narrative): The Process Logic Narrative provides a description of all process interlocks and alarms.  The Logic Narrative is the primary document used for the design of the Logic Diagrams and/or the DCS control logic. Although the logic narrative is considered a process document, in actual practise, it becomes a co-joint effort between the process and control engineers. The specifics of design intent, feasibility and implementation dictate that a good deal of collaboration is required to craft a sufficiently descriptive and complete document.  Modifications, additions and deletions must be originated from this document. The Logic Narrative is used extensively in developing the operations manual. Instrumentation will check the Logic Narrative for Clarity, Simplicity and, Practicality for ease of configuration of a typical DCS system.  Specific interlocking and alarm requirements remain the responsibility of Process. To Section 3.10 (Logic Diagrams): Logic drawings are based on the Logic Narrative and are used in the specific configuration of the control system.  As such they represent the Logic Narrative in another form and are therefore redundant. The trend in control systems is for the software configuration (Operating System), to produce the control configuration documentation package.  Logic drawings will no longer be produced within the scope of projects. This being said, precedent may dictate deliverables. To Section 3.11 (Control System I/O List): The Control System I/O list will be prepared in conjunction with the Instrument Index by the Subcontractor.  A preliminary I/O list will be created during the same time frame as the preliminary Instrument Index.  The I/O list will include individual totals of the various types of I/O required for the project.  When a dual Instrument numbering system is used for the project, the Client’s preferred Instrument numbering will be used. The power supply identified on the I/O list will define whether the Instrument is a 4-wire type device or whether it is a 2-wire type device.  In addition it will define the voltage requirements of the individual device. Control System I/O List will contain all instrumentation and electrical devices that will be monitored and/or controlled directly from the plant control system.  This includes all required electrical monitoring signals from MCC’s, Switchgear, Transformer Rectifiers etc.  Instrument Tags assigned to these monitoring signals are to be shown on a P&ID. Typical Control system wiring will conform to the following: Analog inputs (2-wire/4-wire  4-20 mA) Discrete inputs (Isolated, Dry 120 VAC or 24 VDC) Discrete outputs (Isolated, High Side 120 VAC or 24 VDC) Digital Bus (Profibus, Fieldbus) To Section 3.12 (Electrical System I/O List): Typical Electrical system wiring will conform to the following:

• Analog inputs (2-wire/4-wire  4-20 mA) • Analog outputs (4-20 mA) • Discrete inputs (Isolated, Dry 120 VAC or 24 VDC) • Discrete outputs (Isolated, High Side 120 VAC or 24 VDC) To Section 3.13 (Control Equipment - Cabinet Layouts and Internal Interconnection Wiring): Control Equipment drawings will show the specific special layout for Control Equipment within their designated cabinets.  All equipment will be identified, tagged and dimensioned. The drawings will identify where field devices will interface and indicate the service and type (Analog, Discrete, Digital). Detailed internal Interconnections will be shown in schematic and/or wiring format.  All interface communication connections will be shown.  Responsibility for supply of all communications cabling will be clearly defined. To Section 3.16 (Control System Graphics): Control system graphics will be laid out to provide a logical, efficient and complete interface between the plant operations personnel and the Control system. To reduce confusion, the displayed graphics for monitoring and control details will be kept to a minimum but will be sufficient to allow the operations personnel to completely control the process as intended. The development parameters of these graphics are somewhat subjective. The flexibility and expandability of state of the art systems tends to encourage imagination and personal preference to take a dominance over expedience. Graphics that are aesthetically appealing have an intangible but intrinsic appeal to clients. We want to develop graphics that are simple, logical and minimise frills at the same time they should be visually appealing. Within this environment, standardisation has become a difficult issue to deal with. To Section 3.17 (DCS Operating System Configuration): Due to the unique requirements and proprietary nature of Vendor Control systems, the Vendor, under the direction of the Instrumentation/Electrical Engineer more efficiently sets up the Control System Software Configuration (Operating System).  The documentation of this configuration is usually directly accessible from the Control system itself and will become part of the Control System Manual when the system is installed. To Section 3.18 (Process Control Configuration): The process control configuration (Application Software) will reflect the specific requirements for efficiently controlling and monitoring the process and will be implemented in strict accordance with the logic narrative and logic drawings for the project. Specific interlocks, alarms and trips will be implemented within the configuration as per the Instrument Set Points, Alarms and Interlocks section in the operating manual.
